Why shouldn't I grieve for those who die.label: on death and grief
Why shouldn't I grieve for those who die.answer_html_plain: You shouldn’t grieve for those who die because the wise see that the Self is not destroyed: it is not born, does not die, and continues beyond the body’s destruction. [gita 2.20] [gita 2.12] Therefore Kṛṣṇa says that the paṇḍitāḥ (“the wise,” knowers of the Self) do not grieve for the gatāsūn (“dead, whose breaths have gone”) or the living. [gita 2.11] Textual support: - Kṛṣṇa directly says: “You have grieved for those who are not to be grieved for,” and “the wise do not grieve for the dead … nor for the living.” [gita 2.11] - Śaṅkara explains aśocyāḥ (“not to be grieved for”) as persons like Bhīṣma and Droṇa, because “in their ultimate nature, they are eternal.” [gita 2.11] - The Self undergoes no death: “He is not born, and he does not die, ever,” since birth and final destruction are denied of the Self. [gita 2.20] - Kṛṣṇa also says that “never at any time did I not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men,” and that after the body’s destruction “we all shall never not exist” in ātma-svarūpa (“Self-nature”). [gita 2.12] - Even at the level of embodied life, mṛtyuḥ (“death”) is certain for one born and janma (“birth”) is certain for one dead; because this matter is aparihārya (“inevitable”), you should not grieve. [gita 2.27] - Beings are avyakta (“unmanifest”) before arising, manifest in the middle, and unmanifest again at death; therefore the verse asks, “what lamentation is there?” [gita 2.28]

How do I act without clinging to the fru.label: acting without clinging
How do I act without clinging to the fru.answer_html_plain: Direct answer: perform your karma (“action”) because that is where your adhikāra (“entitlement/field of responsibility”) lies, but do not take yourself to have entitlement over the phala (“fruit/result”); also do not fall into saṅga (“attachment”) to akarman (“non-action”). [gita 2.47] Textual support: - Gītā 2.47 says: “Your entitlement is only with respect to action, never with respect to the fruits,” and adds, “Do not become the cause of obtaining the fruit of action; do not let attachment to non-action be yours.” [gita 2.47] - Śaṅkara on Gītā 2.50 defines kauśalam (“skillfulness”) in action not as ordinary cleverness, but as samatva-buddhi (“equanimity of understanding”) toward siddhi (“success”) and asiddhi (“failure”), while acting with īśvarārpita-cetastā (“the mind offered to Īśvara”). [gita 2.50] - Gītā 2.51 says that the wise, endowed with this equanimous buddhi (“understanding”), abandon the action-born fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth, reaching the affliction-free station called mokṣa (“liberation”). [gita 2.51] - Śaṅkara on Gītā 2.70 adds that when kāmāḥ (“desires”) arise, they enter and dissolve in the self without disturbing the person or bringing him under their control. [gita 2.70]

What does a person of steady wisdom look.label: the person at peace
What does a person of steady wisdom look.answer_html_plain: Directly: A person of steady wisdom, sthitaprajñaḥ (“one whose wisdom is established”), is a wise person whose discriminative knowledge is settled; in daily life he remains unshaken by suffering, without craving amid pleasure, free from attachment, fear, and anger, unattached even to body and life, and able to withdraw the senses from sense-objects like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs. [gita 2.55] [gita 2.56] [gita 2.57] [gita 2.58] Textual support: - Śaṅkara explains sthitaprajñaḥ not as an abstract “steady wisdom,” but as a vidvān (“wise person”) whose wisdom born from discrimination between Self and non-Self is firmly established. [gita 2.55] - In the Gītā’s description, when suffering comes, his mind is anudvigna (“unagitated”); when pleasure comes, his craving is gone; and rāga (“attachment”), bhaya (“fear”), and krodha (“anger”) have departed. [gita 2.56] - Śaṅkara says he is anabhisnehaḥ (“without clinging”) everywhere, even toward body, life, and the like. [gita 2.57] - Śaṅkara also characterizes him as free from joy and sorrow, with discrimination-born wisdom established. [gita 2.57] - Practically, he withdraws the indriyāṇi (“senses”) from indriyārthāḥ (“sense-objects”) on every side, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs. [gita 2.58] - He is also saṃyamī (“self-controlled”): what is “night” to ordinary beings—the ultimate reality—is where he is awake, while what ordinary beings take as wakefulness is “night” to the seeing sage. [gita 2.69]

What happens to the soul when the body d.label: the soul at death
What happens to the soul when the body d.answer_html_plain: According to Śaṅkara’s readings here, when the body dies, the ātmā (“Self/soul”) itself is not destroyed, born, killed, or changed; the changeless dehī (“embodied self”) attains another body (dehāntara-prāptiḥ, “attainment of another body”). [gita 2.13] [gita 2.20] [gita 2.30] In the Īśā commentary, Śaṅkara distinguishes this from the liṅga (“subtle body”): the subtle body, conditioned by knowledge and action, departs, while the gross body becomes ashes. [isa 17] After death (pretya, “having left this body”), beings attain further births/worlds according to karma and what has been heard. [isa 3] Textual support: Śaṅkara says the self is not destroyed when bodily states perish and that another-body attainment belongs to the changeless self. [gita 2.13] He also takes the self as unborn (aja), eternal (nitya), and not killed/changed when the body is killed. [gita 2.20] He explains the embodied one as “unslayable” because partless and eternal, even when the body is being killed. [gita 2.30]

What is yoga, in its oldest technical de.label: what yoga actually means
What is yoga, in its oldest technical de.answer_html_plain: The passages do not provide historical evidence to prove which definition is “oldest.” What they do provide as the technical Yoga-sūtra definition is: yoga (discipline/concentration) is samādhi (meditative absorption), specified as nirodha (restraint/checking) of mental activity—not annihilation of mind [yogasutra 1.1] [yogasutra 1.2]. Textual support: - Vyāsa on Yogasūtra 1.1 states directly: “yogaḥ samādhiḥ” — “Yoga is samādhi” [yogasutra 1.1]. - Vyāsa’s explanation of Yogasūtra 1.2 takes nirodha (“restraint/checking”) broadly: because the word “all” is not stated, even saṃprajñāta yoga (“cognitive/object-supported yoga”) is included [yogasutra 1.2]. - In the highest asaṃprajñāta (“non-cognitive/objectless”) state, “nothing at all is distinctly cognized,” so total cessation belongs especially there [yogasutra 1.2]. - Vyāsa further excludes merely distracted concentration: a samādhi subordinated to distraction “does not fall within the class of yoga” [yogasutra 1.1].

How can a restless mind be made clear an.label: calming a restless mind
How can a restless mind be made clear an.answer_html_plain: Directly: In the Yoga material given, a restless citta (“mind”) is steadied by cultivating the prescribed mental attitude/practice so that it becomes prasanna (“clear/serene”), ekāgra (“one-pointed”), and reaches sthitipada (“a state of steadiness”); by breath practice; by direct meditative fixation on a particular object; and by dhyāna (“meditation”) on a chosen agreeable object [yogasutra 1.33] [yogasutra 1.34] [yogasutra 1.35] [yogasutra 1.39]. Textual support: - Vyāsa says that when one “cultivates in this way,” white dharma arises, the mind becomes clear/serene, and, being clear, becomes one-pointed and steady: “prasannam ekāgraṃ sthitipadaṃ labhate” [yogasutra 1.33]. - The Yoga Sūtra says steadiness may also be brought about through pracchardana and vidhāraṇa—“expulsion and retention”—of prāṇa (“breath”) [yogasutra 1.34]. - Vyāsa says this cittaparikarma (“purification/training of the mind”) uses direct apprehension of some particular object to remove doubt and open into samādhi-prajñā (“insight born of samādhi”), so that faith, energy, memory, and samādhi arise unobstructed [yogasutra 1.35]. - The Yoga Sūtra also gives yathābhimata-dhyāna—meditation on whatever is agreeable or chosen—as a means by which the mind becomes steadied [yogasutra 1.39].

Does the repetition of Om actually do an.label: what Om is for
Does the repetition of Om actually do an.answer_html_plain: Yes—according to the Yoga-sūtra material provided, repetition of Oṃ is not presented as empty sound. The praṇava (“sacred syllable Oṃ”) is Oṃ, and japa (“repetition”) of it is specified as “repetition of the praṇava” [yogasutra 1.27, justification] [yogasutra 1.28, justification]. From that devotion to Īśvara, the stated result is pratyak-cetanā-adhigama (“attainment of inward consciousness,” seeing one’s own nature) and antarāya-abhāva (“absence of obstacles”) [yogasutra 1.29]. In Śaṅkara’s reading of Īśā 17, Oṃ also functions as an oṃ-pratīka (“Oṃ-symbol”) through which Brahman called Agni is invoked; it is not treated as a mere exclamation [isa 17, justification]. However, the Īśā passages provided do not state a result specifically from repeating Oṃ.

What is the role of practice and dispass.label: practice and letting go
What is the role of practice and dispass.answer_html_plain: In Vyāsa’s Yoga account, abhyāsa (“practice”) and vairāgya (“dispassion”) master the citta (“mind”) only together: practice steadies the mind and opens the current of viveka (“discrimination”), while dispassion blocks the current toward viṣaya (“objects”). [yogasutra 1.13, translation] [yogasutra 1.12, justification] [yogasutra 1.12, justification] Textual support: - The sūtra defines abhyāsa as “energetic effort toward steadiness,” i.e. toward sthiti (“steadiness”), the tranquil flow of mind without fluctuations. [yogasutra 1.13, translation] - Vyāsa explains that consciousness is like a river flowing in two directions: toward kaivalya with discrimination, or toward saṃsāra with non-discrimination. [yogasutra 1.12, justification] - In that metaphor, vairāgya makes the object-stream barren, while vivekadarśanābhyāsa (“practice of discriminative seeing”) opens the discrimination-stream. [yogasutra 1.12, justification] - Therefore, cittavṛttinirodha (“cessation of mental fluctuations”) depends on both practice and dispassion, not on either one alone. [yogasutra 1.12, justification] - Vyāsa also describes a “mastery” form of dispassion, vaśīkārasaṃjñā vairāgya, as non-engagement toward objects, empty of taking up or rejecting, arising through seeing defects in objects and discriminative discernment. [yogasutra 1.15, justification] - In Vyāsa’s account of Yoga Sūtra 1.20, after faith, energy, recollection, concentration, and discriminating insight arise, asaṃprajñāta samādhi comes about through practice of that insight and dispassion toward each object. [yogasutra 1.20, justification]

Can I enjoy the world without being owne.label: enjoyment without possession
Can I enjoy the world without being owne.answer_html_plain: Yes—but the provided texts support this as renounced, non-covetous living, not as possessive indulgence. In Śaṅkara’s reading of Īśā 1, the world is to be “covered/enveloped” by the Lord as one’s own Self, lived with tyaktena (“by renunciation/abandonment”), and bhuñjīthāḥ means “protect/maintain,” not “enjoy/eat”; the mantra also says mā gṛdhaḥ (“do not covet”) anyone’s wealth [isa 1, term] [isa 1, justification]. Textual support: Īśā 2 says that, for one living as a nara (“man”), one should live while doing karmāṇi (“works/actions”), and then karma na lipyate—“action does not cling”—to that person [isa 2, translation]. So the answer is: live and act in the world, but through tyāga (“renunciation”) and non-coveting, so that action does not “cling” to you [isa 1, term] [isa 2, translation]. What is not supplied here: the passages do not justify “enjoying the world” in the sense of indulgent possession or consumption; in fact, Śaṅkara’s gloss on Īśā 1 explicitly avoids reading bhuñjīthāḥ as “enjoy/eat” [isa 1, term].

Can knowledge be as dangerous as ignoran.label: when knowledge misleads
Can knowledge be as dangerous as ignoran.answer_html_plain: Yes—but only in Śaṅkara’s technical reading of the Īśā Upaniṣad passage: vidyā (“knowledge,” specifically deity-knowledge) pursued alone leads to “greater darkness,” while avidyā (“ignorance,” here ritual action/karma, not mere psychological ignorance) also leads to darkness when pursued alone [isa 9, term]. Śaṅkara does not mean that liberating knowledge of the supreme Self is dangerous; in these passages, vidyā is devatājñāna (“knowledge concerning deities”) and avidyā is karma (“ritual action,” such as Agnihotra) [isa 11, justification]. The remedy given is to know and use both together: by avidyā/karma one crosses death, and by vidyā/devatājñāna one attains the immortal state of deity-selfhood [isa 11, translation]. So, in this limited Śaṅkara/Īśā context, one-sided “knowledge” can be even more dangerous than one-sided “ignorance/action,” but the passages do not say that liberating Self-knowledge is dangerous [isa 9, term]; [isa 11, justification].

Is it wrong to want to live a hundred ye.label: a long and active life
Is it wrong to want to live a hundred ye.answer_html_plain: No. In Śaṅkara’s reading of Īśā 2, wanting to live a hundred years is not condemned; jijīviṣet (“one should wish to live”) is treated as a prāptānuvāda (“restatement of an already-natural fact”), while the actual injunction is to live while doing karmāṇi (“scripture-enjoined ritual works,” especially Agnihotra and the like) [isa 2, justification] [isa 2, justification]. Textually, Īśā 2 says: “Only doing here the ritual works, one should seek to live a hundred years,” and adds that for such a nara (“man,” i.e. one identifying as merely human and wishing to live), “there is no other way” by which karma (“action”) does not cling [isa 2, translation] [isa 2, justification]. So, on the provided Śaṅkara material: the wish for long life is natural, not itself made an independent duty or treated as wrong; what is prescribed for the one who wants to live is performing the śāstra-enjoined works [isa 2, justification] [isa 2, justification].

Does the external world really exist out.label: is the world in the mind?
Does the external world really exist out.answer_html_plain: Direct answer: For Sthiramati on the Triṃśikā, the external world as an object outside consciousness does not really exist; what really exists is vijñāna-pariṇāma (“transformation of consciousness”), while the imagined object-domain is absent. [trimsika 1, justification] [trimsika 17, justification] Textual support: - Sthiramati says that self and dharmas do not exist outside vijñāna-pariṇāma (“transformation of consciousness”), and that this transformation must be accepted as really existing as the basis for imputation. [trimsika 1, justification] - Sthiramati says that whatever is imagined by vikalpa (“construction”)—including the receptacle-world, self, aggregates, elements, sense-bases, form, sound, and so on—does not exist. [trimsika 17, justification] - Sthiramati explains this as viṣaya-abhāva (“absence of an object-domain”): because the imagined object is absent, everything is vijñapti-mātra (“representation-only”). [trimsika 17, justification] - Sthiramati also argues that consciousness can arise in illusion, dream, and eye-disease even when the object is unreal, so consciousness arises from a prior consciousness of the same kind, not from an external object. [trimsika 17, justification] - Sthiramati says cognition does not apprehend anything bahiś cittāt (“outside mind”); it does not see, grasp, or fixate on anything outside mind. [trimsika 28, justification] So, in these passages, the answer is: not as an external reality outside consciousness; the “external world” is an imagined object-domain, while consciousness-transformation is the real dependent basis. [trimsika 1, justification] [trimsika 17, justification]

Does karma leave impressions in the mind.label: the seeds karma leaves
Does karma leave impressions in the mind.answer_html_plain: Yes—according to Sthiramati on the Triṃśikā, karma leaves karmavāsanāḥ (“karmic impressions/capacities”) deposited in ālayavijñāna (“storehouse consciousness”), not merely a vague trace in an unspecified mind. [trimsika 19] Textual support: Sthiramati defines karmavāsanā as the capacity deposited in ālayavijñāna by karma for producing a future embodied existence. [trimsika 19] He also says that kuśala/akuśala-karmavāsanā (“impressions of wholesome/unwholesome karma”) ripen and produce vipāka (“maturation-result”). [trimsika 2] These karmic impressions generate further maturation when accompanied by grāhadvayavāsanā (“impression of the twofold grasping”). [trimsika 19] The passages do not state that karma leaves impressions in every kind of “mind”; they specifically give ālayavijñāna as the locus. [trimsika 19]

Does consciousness continue in dreamless.label: the mind in deep sleep
Does consciousness continue in dreamless.answer_html_plain: Direct answer: According to Vyāsa on the Yogasūtra, yes: nidrā (“sleep,” contrasted with svapna “dream”) is a pratyayaviśeṣa (“particular cognition”), not a blank absence of cognition [yogasutra 1.38] [yogasutra 1.10]. According to Sthiramati on the Triṃśikā, manovijñāna (“mental consciousness”) does not continue in acittaka middha (“mindless torpor/sleep”), but ālayavijñāna (“store-consciousness”) continues as a stream and is the source from which mental consciousness arises again [trimsika 16, justification] [trimsika 4]. Textual support: - Vyāsa distinguishes svapna-jñāna (“dream-cognition”) from nidrā-jñāna (“sleep-cognition”), so the passages treat sleep as distinct from dream [yogasutra 1.38]. - Vyāsa says sleep is a pratyayaviśeṣa (“particular cognition”) because on waking there is pratyavamarśa (“retrospective awareness”); without an experienced pratyaya (“cognition/presentation”), such recollection would not occur [yogasutra 1.10]. - Sthiramati says manovijñāna-pravṛtti (“occurrence/activity of mental consciousness”) is absent in five exceptional states, including acittaka middha (“mindless torpor/sleep”) [trimsika 16, justification] [trimsika 16, term]. - Sthiramati also says that when manovijñāna has ceased in such states, it arises again only from ālayavijñāna (“store-consciousness”) [trimsika 16, justification]. - The Triṃśikā passages describe ālayavijñāna as “always” accompanied by mental factors and as continuing “in a stream-continuum, like a flood” [trimsika 3, justification] [trimsika 4]. What is missing: the provided passages do not explicitly use the English phrase “dreamless sleep”; they discuss nidrā (“sleep”) in contrast with svapna (“dream”) and acittaka middha (“mindless torpor/sleep”) [yogasutra 1.38] [trimsika 16, term].

What are the seven chakras?.label: not covered — watch it refuse
What are the seven chakras?.answer_html_plain: The provided passages do not answer this. What is missing is any passage that names or lists the seven cakras (“wheels” or energy centers) or describes their locations. The supplied passages instead discuss topics such as sorrow and delusion in Īśā 7 [isa 7, justification], ālayavijñāna (“storehouse consciousness”) in Sthiramati’s Triṃśikā commentary [trimsika 4, justification], yoga-kṣema (“acquisition and safeguarding”) in Gītā 2.45 [gita 2.45, justification], and vastuśūnya (“empty of a corresponding object/reality”) in Yogasūtra 1.9 [yogasutra 1.9, justification].
